items.title: Encounter the Phenomenon: At a recycling plant, a large electromagnet hanging over a conveyor lifts steel cans out of a mixed stream, but a small magnet from a toy cannot do this job. What makes the plant's electromagnet so much stronger?

body.html: The plant magnet is a coil of heavy wire wound many times around an iron core and connected to a power supply. The toy magnet is a small permanent magnet. Find the reason for the difference in strength.

A permanent magnet gets its field only from permanently aligned domains. A coil's field comes from the electric current in it, and that field grows with the current, with the number of loops, and with how closely the loops are packed. An iron core is magnetized by the coil and adds its own field.

The plant magnet can carry a large current through hundreds of tightly packed loops, so the fields of all the loops add inside the coil. The coil's field lines up the domains of the iron core, which adds a much larger field of its own. The toy magnet has a fixed, small field with nothing that can be increased.

answer.html: The plant magnet is stronger because a large current flows through many closely spaced loops around an iron core, whose domains line up with the coil's field. Each factor increases the field beyond what a small permanent magnet supplies.

items.title: Science and Engineering Practice: Ask Questions

question.html: Do you have other questions about the phenomenon? (Open-ended; sample questions are given below.)

answer.html: (1) By how much does the lifting force change if the current is doubled? (2) Does the steel core stay magnetized after the power is switched off? (3) Why are aluminum cans left on the belt while steel cans are lifted? (4) How would the plant make the magnet work from farther away? Your own questions will differ; any question that can be investigated with the ideas in this module works.

items.title: Focus Question: Why do a steel nail and an iron bolt cling to a magnet, while a copper pipe and a plastic spoon do not?

body.html: Ferromagnetic materials (iron, nickel, cobalt, and alloys such as steel) have atoms that act like tiny magnets and group into domains. A magnet can line those domains up. Copper and plastic have no such domains.

The magnet's field aligns the domains in the nail and the bolt, which then become temporary magnets, and the unlike poles near each other attract. In copper and plastic nothing aligns, so there is no attraction.

answer.html: The nail and bolt are ferromagnetic, so their domains line up in the magnet's field and they are attracted. Copper and plastic do not form aligned domains, so they feel no magnetic attraction.

items.title: Get It? (p. 548): Give examples of how humans use Earth's magnetic field for modern travel and science

body.html: Earth acts as a huge magnet, so a free magnetic needle lines up with its field.

A magnetic compass gives direction to pilots, boaters, and hikers where no landmarks are available. Geologists measure the direction in which iron minerals were magnetized in old lava flows to learn how the field and the continents have changed.

answer.html: Magnetic compasses for navigation in aircraft, boats, and on foot, and studying the magnetization of ancient rock to reconstruct past positions of Earth's poles.

items.title: Get It? (p. 549): Cite Evidence: what do the domains look like in a steel paper clip that has just been pulled off a strong magnet and now holds a second clip?

body.html: An object that attracts other ferromagnetic objects must have a net magnetic field, which requires that many of its domains point the same way.
The first clip holds the second, so it is a magnet right now. A random arrangement of domains would have fields that cancel and could not hold anything.

answer.html: Most of the domains in the clip point the same direction, so their small fields add into a net field strong enough to hold the second clip.

items.title: Figure 3 caption (p. 549): A bar magnet is held by its north pole, and its south pole touches the head of an iron nail. Identify the poles of the nail

body.html: The magnet's south pole touches the nail's head. The nail's point hangs downward with a small steel tack stuck to it. Find the poles at the head and at the point.
A magnet polarizes an iron object by induction, so the end of the nail nearest the magnet becomes a pole opposite to the touching pole, because unlike poles attract.
The magnet's south pole touches the head, so the head becomes a north pole. The point at the other end becomes a south pole, and it is this south pole that holds the tack.

answer.html: The head of the nail is a north pole and the point is a south pole.

items.title: Check The point is a pole itself, which explains why it can attract and hold the tack. Practice Problems (Lesson 1, Problems 1–4) Problem 1 (Lesson 1 Practice): Will the force between two bar magnets be attractive or repulsive when (a) the south pole of one is brought near the north pole of the other, and (b) the south pole of one is brought near the south pole of the other?

body.html: (a) south pole near north pole, (b) south pole near south pole. Find the type of force.
Like poles repel; unlike poles attract.
(a) A south pole and a north pole are unlike poles. (b) Two south poles are like poles.

answer.html: (a) Attractive. (b) Repulsive.

items.title: Check Reversing one of the magnets in (a) would make both poles south, giving the repulsion of (b). Problem 2 (Lesson 1 Practice): Six disk magnets float in a vertical stack on a plastic rod, each hovering above the one below. The top face of the top disk is a south pole. What pole is on the top face of each of the other five disks?

body.html: Six disks float one above another. The top face of disk 1 (the top disk) is S. Find the top-face pole of disks 2 through 6.
A disk floats only if the one below pushes up on it, so the facing sides of neighboring disks must be like poles. Each disk has opposite poles on its two faces.

Disk 1: top S, so bottom N. Disk 2's top face faces that N, so it is N, and its bottom is S. Disk 3's top face faces S, so it is S, and its bottom is N. Disk 4's top is N and its bottom is S. Disk 5's top is S and its bottom is N. Disk 6's top is N.

answer.html: From the top down, the top faces are S (given), N, S, N, S, N. So disks 2 through 6 have N, S, N, S, N on top.

items.title: Check Each pair of facing sides is like poles (N–N or S–S), so every pair repels and the stack floats. Problem 3 (Lesson 1 Practice): Earth's geographic north region is near a magnetic south pole. Explain why the end of a hiker's compass needle that points toward the Arctic is labeled N.

body.html: Unlike poles attract, and a compass needle is a small magnet free to rotate.

The needle points toward the Arctic because that end is attracted to the magnetic south pole of Earth located there. Only a north pole is attracted to a south pole. So the end that points toward the Arctic is a magnetic north pole, and it is named "north-seeking," or N.

answer.html: The end of the needle that swings toward the Arctic is attracted to Earth's magnetic south pole there, so it must be a magnetic north pole, and it is labeled N.

items.title: Check If that end were a south pole it would be repelled from the Arctic and would point away from it. Problem 4 (Lesson 1 Practice, Challenge): After lightning struck close to a boat, the crew found that the compass needle's N end now points south. Explain.

body.html: A strong field can rearrange the domains of a ferromagnetic needle, and a needle stays magnetized when its domains remain aligned.

A lightning strike carries an enormous current, and a current produces a magnetic field. Near the strike that field was far stronger than Earth's and could line up the needle's domains the opposite way, reversing its poles. The end labeled N became a south pole. A south pole is attracted to Earth's magnetic north pole, which is near the geographic south, so the labeled N end now points south.

answer.html: The strong magnetic field of the lightning current re-magnetized the needle and reversed its poles, so the end labeled N is now a south pole and points south.

items.title: Get It? and prompts on magnetic fields and the discovery of current's field Oersted summary (Get It?, p. 553): A student closes a switch and a compass near a wire swings away from north; opening the switch lets it swing back. Summarize in your own words what this shows

answer.html: A wire carrying current produces a magnetic field around it. The compass needle, which responds only to magnetic fields, turned only while current flowed, so the current must have made the field.

items.title: Analyze (Figure 10 margin): A long wire carries current to the north and the field above the wire points east. The current is reversed and its size is doubled. What happens to the field?

body.html: The right-hand rule fixes the field direction from the current direction, and the field strength is proportional to the current.
Reversing the current reverses which way the fingers curl around the wire, so the field above the wire now points west. Doubling the current doubles the field strength.

answer.html: The field above the wire reverses to point west, and it is twice as strong.

items.title: Assess (Figure 11 margin): A solenoid's loops are pushed closer together with the current unchanged. How does the field inside change, and is it greater inside or outside the coil?

body.html: Inside a solenoid the fields of all loops add; the more loops per unit length, the stronger the field.

With the loops closer together, there are more loops in each centimeter of the coil, so more fields add and the field inside gets stronger. The lines inside are packed together, and outside they spread through a large space, so the field is greater inside.

answer.html: The field inside gets stronger. It is greater inside the solenoid than outside.

items.title: CCC Cause and Effect (p. 553): A student sets up a compass beside a straight wire. List the observations that would show that current produces a magnetic field

answer.html: (1) With the switch open, the needle lines up with Earth's field and does not point toward or away from the wire. (2) With the switch closed, the needle turns to a new direction, perpendicular to the wire. (3) If the compass is moved to the other side of the wire, or the battery is reversed, the needle turns the opposite way. (4) When the switch is opened, the needle returns to its original direction. Because the needle responds only to magnetic fields and changes only while current flows, the current must produce the field.

items.title: Practice Problems (Lesson 1, Problems 5–9) Problem 5 (Lesson 1 Practice): How does the magnetic field 4 cm from a long straight current-carrying wire compare with the field at (a) 2 cm and (b) 6 cm?

body.html: 𝑟<sub>1</sub> = 4 cm; compare with 𝑟<sub>2</sub> = 2 cm and 𝑟<sub>3</sub> = 6 cm.
The field around a long straight wire is inversely proportional to the distance from it: 𝐵∝1 / 𝑟.
<sup>𝐵</sup><sup>1</sup> <sup>𝐵</sup><sub>2</sub> =<sup> </sup><sup>𝑟</sup><sup>2</sup>
<sub>4</sub><sub> </sub><sub>cm</sub> = 0.5 and <sup>𝐵</sup><sup>1</sup>

answer.html: (a) The field at 4 cm is half as strong as at 2 cm. (b) The field at 4 cm is 1.5 times as strong as at 6 cm.

items.title: 6 (Lesson 1 Practice): A long straight wire runs east-west. (a) The north pole of a compass held above the wire points south. What is the direction of the current? (b) Which way would a compass below the wire point?

body.html: Use the right-hand rule: thumb along the conventional current, fingers curl in the direction of the field. A compass's north pole points along the field.
(a) The field above the wire is south. Point the right thumb east and curl the fingers: over the top of the wire they go toward the south. So the current is east.
(b) On the other side of the wire the circle runs the opposite way, so the field below the wire points north.

answer.html: (a) The current flows east. (b) The compass below the wire points north (its north pole points north).

items.title: Check The fields above and below a wire are always opposite, so south above means north below. Problem 7 (Lesson 1 Practice): A nail is wrapped with insulated wire connected to a battery. Looking from the head of the nail toward its point, the current circulates counterclockwise around the nail. Which end of the nail (head or point) is the north pole?

body.html: The current circles counterclockwise when viewed from the head end looking toward the point. Find the end that is the north pole.
Use the solenoid right-hand rule: curl the fingers of the right hand in the direction of the current, and the thumb points toward the north pole.

Counterclockwise as seen by a viewer looking along the nail from the head toward the point means that the right-hand thumb points toward the viewer, which is toward the head. So the thumb, and the north pole, is at the head. The point is the south pole.

answer.html: The head of the nail is the north pole (the point is the south pole).

items.title: Check Reversing the battery would reverse the current direction and swap the poles. Problem 8 (Lesson 1 Practice): You have a battery, insulated wire, a wooden pencil, a steel bolt, and a brass rod. Which would you wind the wire around to make an electromagnet that picks up paper clips best?

body.html: A ferromagnetic core is magnetized by the coil's field and strengthens it greatly. Wood and brass are not ferromagnetic.

The wire wound around any of the three and connected to the battery makes a solenoid. Only steel is ferromagnetic, so the steel's domains line up with the coil's field and add to it. Wood and brass add nothing noticeable.

answer.html: The steel bolt. The coil's field aligns its domains, so it becomes a strong temporary magnet that can pick up paper clips.

items.title: Check Without a ferromagnetic core, the coil alone would pick up much less. Problem 9 (Lesson 1 Practice, Challenge): A 12-V supply is connected to an electromagnet coil of resistance 6.0 Ω, giving a field strength proportional to the current. A variable resistor is placed in series with the coil. What resistance must be added to cut the field strength in half, and how does this relate to 𝐼= 𝑉/ 𝑅?

body.html: 𝑉= 12 V, 𝑅<sub>coil</sub> = 6.0 𝛺. The field is proportional to the current. Find the added resistance 𝑅<sub>add</sub> for half the field.
Ohm's law 𝐼= 𝑉/ 𝑅<sub>total</sub>, with series resistances adding. Half the field requires half the current.

Initially 𝐼<sub>1</sub> =<sup> </sup><sup>12</sup><sup> </sup><sup>V</sup> <sub>6.0</sub><sub> </sub><sub>𝛺</sub>= 2.0 A. Half the field means 𝐼<sub>2</sub> = 1.0 A. Then 𝑅<sub>total</sub> =<sup> </sup><sup>12</sup><sup> </sup><sup>V</sup> <sub>1.0</sub><sub> </sub><sub>A</sub> = 12 𝛺, so 𝑅<sub>add</sub> = 12 𝛺−6.0 𝛺= 6.0 𝛺.

answer.html: Add 6.0 𝛺 in series with the coil. The variable resistor changes the current, and the field is proportional to the current.

items.title: Check The total resistance doubled (6.0 Ω to 12 Ω), so the current and the field are cut in half. Check Your Progress (Lesson 1, Problems 10–18) Problem 10 (Check Your Progress): List four changes that would make a homemade electromagnet stronger.

answer.html: (1) Increase the current (a stronger battery or less added resistance). (2) Use more loops of wire. (3) Wind the loops closer together. (4) Put an iron core inside the coil. Each makes the field inside the coil stronger.

items.title: 11 (Check Your Progress): In a sketch of a magnet's field, the lines are crowded together near one end and far apart near the other end. What does this tell you about the field, and what else do the lines show?

answer.html: The field is strong where the lines are crowded and weak where they are far apart, so the line spacing shows strength. The arrows on the lines show the direction of the field (the direction a compass north pole would point), out of north poles and into south poles.

items.title: 12 (Check Your Progress): A magnet pulls a steel paper clip from 2 cm away, with nothing between them. A friend says that nothing is touching the clip, so there cannot be a force. Use fields to respond.

answer.html: The magnet sets up a magnetic field in the space around it. The clip is in that field, and the field at the clip's location exerts the force on it, so no contact is needed. The field carries the interaction through space.

items.title: 13 (Check Your Progress): Where is the magnetic field strongest around a horseshoe magnet?

answer.html: At the two ends (the poles), especially in the gap between them where the field lines are most closely packed.

items.title: 14 (Check Your Progress): Two long parallel vertical wires, one west of the other, carry equal currents. Look down from above, with north at the top of the page. Point M is midway between the wires and point Q is east of both wires. Describe the field at M and at Q if the currents are (a) both upward, (b) one upward (west wire) and one downward (east wire).

body.html: Fields from separate wires add as vectors. A current toward the viewer (upward, seen from above) has a counterclockwise field, and a current away from the viewer (downward) has a clockwise field. Field strength is greater closer to a wire.

(a) Both currents toward the viewer. At M, east of the west wire, its counterclockwise field points north; the east wire's field at M (on its west side) points south. They cancel exactly at the midpoint. At Q, east of both, both fields point north, so they add.

(b) The west wire's current is toward the viewer, so at M its field points north. The east wire's current is away from the viewer (clockwise), so at M, on its west side, its field points north as well. They add. At Q, the west wire's field points north, but the east wire's field points south and the east wire is nearer, so the fields partly cancel and the net field is weak and points south.

answer.html: (a) At M the fields cancel (zero field); at Q they add and the field is north. (b) At M the fields add and the field is strong, pointing north; at Q they partly cancel, leaving a weak field pointing south.

items.title: Check The two cases are mirror images of each other, so what cancels in one adds in the other. Problem 15 (Check Your Progress): A vertical wire carries current upward. Use the right-hand rule to find the direction in which the field circulates around the wire as seen from above, and state the rule.

answer.html: Grasp the wire with your right hand with your thumb pointing in the direction of the conventional current (upward). Your fingers curl in the direction of the field. Seen from above, the fingers curl counterclockwise, so the field circulates counterclockwise.

items.title: 16 (Check Your Progress): Iron filings sprinkled on a card over an electromagnet form a pattern. The current is then reversed and doubled. What differences do you expect in the pattern?

body.html: Reversing the current reverses the field direction, but a filing lines up along the field line in either sense. Doubling the current doubles the field strength.

The shape of the field is the same, with only the arrowheads reversed, and the filings have no arrowheads, so the shape of the pattern does not change. A stronger field magnetizes the filings more and pulls more of them into lines.

answer.html: The pattern has the same shape (the reversal cannot be seen in filings), but the lines of filings are sharper and more filings are drawn in because the field is twice as strong.

items.title: 17 (Check Your Progress): A soft iron nail is touched to a magnet and picks up a paper clip. When the nail is pulled away from the magnet, the clip falls. Explain with domains.

answer.html: While touching the magnet, the nail's domains line up with the magnet's field, so the nail is a temporary magnet and holds the clip. When it is pulled away, the domains return to a random arrangement, their fields cancel, and the nail loses its magnetism, so the clip falls.

items.title: 18 (Check Your Progress, Critical Thinking): A toy has ring magnets on a vertical wooden spindle Problem 18(a): A top ring hovers above the lower ring, but when the top ring is flipped over it drops down onto the lower ring. Explain.

body.html: Rings that attract or repel without other help are permanent magnets, and the force depends on which poles face each other.

The top ring hovers because the lower ring repels it: like poles face each other, and the repulsion supports its weight. Flipping the ring swaps its faces, so unlike poles face each other, they attract, and the ring drops.

answer.html: Both rings are permanent magnets. When like poles face, the repulsion holds the top ring up. Flipping it makes unlike poles face, which attract, so it falls onto the lower ring.

items.title: 18(b): A replacement top ring falls onto the lower one in either orientation, and it picks up no paper clips. What kind of material is it?

body.html: An unmagnetized ferromagnetic object is attracted by either pole of a magnet, because the magnet induces an opposite pole on the nearest face.
The ring is attracted either way, so it has no poles of its own, and it picks up no clips, so it is not a magnet.

answer.html: An unmagnetized ferromagnetic material such as soft iron or steel, a temporary magnet by induction, not a permanent magnet.

items.title: Encounter the Phenomenon: What makes this electromagnet stronger than a typical refrigerator magnet?

body.html: A refrigerator magnet is a permanent magnet whose field comes only from aligned domains in the material. An electromagnet's field comes from an electric current in a coil (solenoid), and that field can be made far larger.

The field of a solenoid grows with the current, with the number of loops, and with how closely the loops are packed. An iron core adds to this, because the coil's field aligns the iron's domains and the iron becomes a strong temporary magnet. A large electromagnet can carry a large current through many loops around an iron core, so its field is much greater than the field of a small permanent magnet.

answer.html: The electromagnet is stronger because a large current flows through many closely spaced loops, usually around an iron core whose domains line up with the coil's field. Each of those factors increases the field beyond what a small permanent magnet can supply.

items.title: Science and Engineering Practice: Ask Questions

question.html: Do you have other questions about the phenomenon? (Open-ended; sample questions are given below.)

answer.html: (1) How does the strength of the field depend on the current and on the number of loops? (2) Why does an iron core make the magnet stronger? (3) How can the magnet release the metal when the current is turned off? (4) Why does scrap steel stick but aluminum cans do not? Your own questions will differ; any question that can be investigated with the ideas in this module works.

items.title: Focus Question: Why are some materials magnetic and others are not?

question.html: Some materials (iron, nickel, cobalt) are ferromagnetic: their atoms act like tiny magnets and group into domains in which the atoms' poles are aligned. In a magnetized piece of ferromagnetic material most domains point the same way, so their fields add. In materials like brass, copper, and aluminum, the atoms do not form such aligned domains, so these materials show essentially no magnetism and are not attracted to magnets.

answer.html: Only ferromagnetic materials (iron, nickel, cobalt, and their alloys) have domains that can line up and make the material a magnet; other materials do not form aligned domains.

items.title: Get It? (p. 548): Examples of how humans have used Earth's magnetic poles

question.html: People used Earth's magnetism to navigate: ancient sailors used lodestones (naturally magnetic magnetite) as compasses, and compasses today still point toward Earth's geographic north because it lies near a magnetic pole. Scientists also use magnetic domains in seafloor rocks as a record of Earth's past field.

answer.html: Navigation with lodestones and compasses (on ships, in aircraft, and on hikes), and studying seafloor rocks to learn that Earth's poles have reversed many times.

items.title: Get It? (p. 549): Cite Evidence: what do the domains look like in the magnet on the first page of the module?

question.html: The opener shows a magnet picking up scrap metal, so the magnet is strongly magnetized. A strongly magnetized material has most of its domains pointing in the same direction.

answer.html: The domains in the magnet are mostly lined up in the same direction (not random), so their small fields add together to make a strong overall field.

items.title: Figure 3 caption (p. 549): Identify the north and south poles of the nail

question.html: What we know The magnet's north pole is the red end, marked N, which is in the hand. Its south pole is the dark end, and the south pole touches the nail (the metal rod carrying the paper clips). Physics idea A magnet polarizes a ferromagnetic object by induction, aligning its domains with the magnet's field. The end of the nail nearest the magnet is a pole opposite to the magnet's touching pole, since unlike poles attract. Work The magnet's south pole touches the nail. The nail's end touching it becomes a north pole. The far end, where the paper clips hang, becomes a south pole.

answer.html: The end of the nail touching the magnet is a north pole, and the far end (with the clips) is a south pole.

items.title: Practice Problems (Lesson 1, Problems 1–4, p. 550) Problem 1 (Lesson 1 Practice) Will the force between two bar magnets be attractive or repulsive in (a) and (b)?

body.html: (a) north pole near north pole, (b) north pole near south pole. Find the type of force.
Like poles repel; unlike poles attract.
(a) Two north poles are like poles. (b) A north and a south pole are unlike poles.

answer.html: (a) Repulsive. (b) Attractive.

items.title: Check This matches Figure 2: like poles pushed apart and unlike poles pulled together. Problem 2 (Lesson 1 Practice) Which poles are on the top side of each of the other four floating disk magnets? (Figure 5)

body.html: Five disk magnets float one above another and the top face of the top disk is a north pole. Find the top-face pole of the other four disks.
A magnet floats only if the magnet below pushes up on it, so the facing sides of any two neighbors must be like poles (repulsion). Each disk has opposite poles on its two faces.

Disk 1 (top): top face N, so bottom face S. Disk 2's top face faces that bottom face and must repel it, so it is S, and its bottom face is N. Disk 3's top face faces N, so it is N and its bottom is S. Disk 4's top is S and its bottom is N. Disk 5's top is N.

answer.html: From the top down, the top faces are N (given), S, N, S, N. The second disk has S on top, the third has N, the fourth has S, and the fifth has N.

items.title: Check Each pair of facing sides is like poles (S–S or N–N), so each pair repels, which is why they float. Problem 3 (Lesson 1 Practice) Explain why the end of a compass needle marked N points north.

body.html: Earth acts like a giant magnet. Unlike poles attract.

The needle is a small magnet free to rotate. Its marked N end is the "north-seeking" pole, so it is a magnetic north pole. A magnetic north pole is attracted to a magnetic south pole. Earth's magnetic south pole is located near the geographic North Pole. So the needle's N end swings toward the geographic north.

answer.html: The needle's N end is a magnetic north pole. It is attracted to the magnetic south pole of Earth, which lies near the geographic North Pole, so it points north.

items.title: Check The compass needle is a magnet itself, so it must follow the like-repel/unlike-attract rule. Problem 4 (Lesson 1 Practice, Challenge) Why might a compass point south after a magnet is touched to it?

body.html: A strong magnet changes the alignment of domains in a ferromagnetic needle, and a needle's magnetism is permanent if its domains stay aligned.

When a magnet touches the needle, its field is much stronger than Earth's. It can rearrange the needle's domains so that the needle's poles are reversed (the end that used to be N becomes S). The needle then keeps that new magnetization. The end marked N is now a south pole, so it is attracted to Earth's magnetic north pole (near the geographic South Pole), and it points south.

answer.html: The touching magnet re-magnetized the needle and reversed its poles, so the end labeled N is now a south pole, and it points south.

items.title: Get It? and prompts on magnetic fields and Oersted (pp. 553) Oersted summary (Get It?, p. 553): Summarize Oersted's conclusion in your own words

answer.html: Oersted concluded that an electric current produces a magnetic field around the wire: the compass needle moved when current flowed, reversed with the current, and went back when the current stopped.

items.title: Analyze (Figure 10 margin): What happens to the magnetic field around a wire when the current changes direction?

question.html: By the right-hand rule, the direction of the field depends on the direction of the current. Reversing the current reverses which way the fingers curl around the wire.

answer.html: The field keeps the same shape and strength but reverses direction (it circulates the opposite way around the wire).

items.title: Assess (Figure 11 margin): Is the magnetic field greater inside or outside the solenoid?

question.html: Inside the coil the fields of all the loops point in the same direction and add, and the field lines are packed closely together. Outside, the lines are spread out over a large space (and the fields of the opposite sides of loops largely oppose).

answer.html: The field is greater inside the solenoid.

items.title: CCC Cause and Effect (p. 553): What empirical evidence did Oersted observe that led him to conclude current produces a magnetic field?

answer.html: With the current off, the compass needle was parallel to the wire. With the current on, the needle turned to be perpendicular to the wire; it pointed the opposite way when the compass was placed on the other side of the wire or when the current was reversed; and it returned to its original position when the current was turned off. Because the needle (affected only by magnetic fields) responded only while current flowed, the current must have produced a magnetic field.

items.title: Practice Problems (Lesson 1, Problems 5–9, p. 555) Problem 5 (Lesson 1 Practice) How does the field 1 cm from a current-carrying wire compare with the field at (a) 2 cm and (b) 3 cm?

body.html: 𝑟<sub>1</sub> = 1 cm; compare with 𝑟<sub>2</sub> = 2 cm and 𝑟<sub>3</sub> = 3 cm.
The field around a long straight wire is inversely proportional to distance: 𝐵∝1 / 𝑟.
<sup>𝐵</sup><sup>1</sup> <sup>𝐵</sup><sub>2</sub> =<sup> </sup><sup>𝑟</sup><sup>2</sup>
<sub>1</sub><sub> </sub><sub>cm</sub> = 2 and <sup>𝐵</sup><sup>1</sup>

answer.html: (a) The field at 1 cm is 2 times as strong as at 2 cm. (b) The field at 1 cm is 3 times as strong as at 3 cm.

items.title: Check Moving farther from the wire weakens the field, so the nearer point must have the larger field. Problem 6 (Lesson 1 Practice) Long straight wire lies north-south. (a) The compass N pole above the wire points east: what is the current direction? (b) Which way does a compass below the wire point?

body.html: The field circles the wire; use the right-hand rule: thumb along the current, fingers curl in the direction of the field. A compass's north pole points along the field.

(a) The field above the wire is east. Point your right thumb north and curl your fingers: over the top of the wire they go toward the east, and under the wire they go toward the west. So the current is north.
(b) On the other side of the wire the circle runs in the opposite sense, so the field below the wire is west.

answer.html: (a) The current flows north. (b) The compass needle below the wire points west (its north pole points west).

items.title: Check The fields above and below a wire are always opposite, so east above implies west below. Problem 7 (Lesson 1 Practice) Which end of the nail (pointed end or head) is the north pole? (Figure 13)

body.html: The battery's positive terminal is on the right and the negative is on the left. The nail's head is on the left, the point is on the right. The visible parts of the coil on the front of the nail slant from lower left to upper right. Find the nail's north pole.
Conventional current flows out of the positive terminal. Use the solenoid right-hand rule: curl the fingers of the right hand in the direction of the current; the thumb points toward the north pole.

Current leaves the positive terminal (right), travels up the right-hand wire, and goes into the coil at the pointed end. The coil's front strands slant from lower left to upper right, so as the current moves from right to left along the nail it goes down across the front of the nail and up across the back. Curling the right-hand fingers down in front and up behind, the thumb points toward the right, toward the pointed end.

answer.html: The pointed end of the nail is the north pole (the head is the south pole).

items.title: Check The current direction is set by the battery. If the battery were reversed, the poles would swap. Problem 8 (Lesson 1 Practice) With a battery, wire, a glass rod, an iron rod, and an aluminum rod, which rod would make an electromagnet that picks up steel objects?

body.html: A solenoid's field is strengthened by a ferromagnetic core, which is magnetized by induction. Glass and aluminum are not ferromagnetic.

Winding the wire around any of the rods and connecting the battery gives a solenoid. Only the iron core is ferromagnetic, so its domains align with the coil's field, which greatly increases the total field. Glass and aluminum do not add any field (and the glass is an insulator in any case).

answer.html: The iron rod. The coil's field aligns the iron's domains, so the iron becomes a strong temporary magnet and the combined field can pick up steel objects.

items.title: Check Without the iron core the coil's field would be weak, as for a glass or aluminum core. Problem 9 (Lesson 1 Practice, Challenge) Can a potentiometer (variable resistor) be used to adjust the electromagnet's strength?

body.html: The coil's field is proportional to the current in it, and by Ohm's law the current in a circuit is 𝐼= 𝑉/ 𝑅.

Put the potentiometer in series with the battery and coil. Increasing its resistance reduces the current (the battery's potential difference stays about the same), which reduces the field. Decreasing its resistance increases the current and the field.

answer.html: Yes. With the potentiometer in series with the coil, changing its resistance changes the current, and the field strength is proportional to the current.

items.title: Check At the highest resistance the field is weakest, as expected. Check Your Progress (Lesson 1, Problems 10–18, p. 555) Problem 10 (Check Your Progress) Explain how to construct an electromagnet.

answer.html: Wind a long insulated wire into many closely spaced loops (a solenoid), preferably around an iron rod or nail, and connect its ends to a battery or other source of current. The current in the coil makes a magnetic field that is stronger with more current, more loops, closer spacing, and an iron core.

items.title: 11 (Check Your Progress) What two things about a magnetic field can field lines represent?

answer.html: Field lines show the direction of the field (the direction a compass north pole would point, out of north poles and into south poles) and the strength of the field (the closer together the lines, the stronger the field).

items.title: 12 (Check Your Progress) Considering magnetic forces, how are forces at a distance explained?

answer.html: A magnet (or current) sets up a magnetic field in the space around it. Another magnet or moving charge in that space feels a force from the field at its own location, so no direct contact is required: the field carries the interaction through space.

items.title: 13 (Check Your Progress) Where on a bar magnet is the magnetic field strongest?

answer.html: At the poles (the ends), where the field lines are most concentrated.

items.title: 14 (Check Your Progress) Two parallel, nearby wires carry equal currents. How are the fields affected if the currents are (a) in the same direction, (b) in opposite directions?

body.html: Fields from separate wires add as vectors. The field direction around each wire is given by the right-hand rule.

(a) Same direction: between the wires the two fields point in opposite directions, so they partly cancel (and cancel exactly midway between). Outside the pair, both fields point the same way, so they add. (b) Opposite directions: between the wires the fields point the same way, so they add and the field there is strong. Outside the pair the fields are opposite and partly cancel.

answer.html: (a) Same direction: the fields cancel between the wires and add outside them. (b) Opposite directions: the fields add between the wires and cancel outside them.

items.title: Check The two cases are mirror images of each other, so the result in one is the reverse of the other. Problem 15 (Check Your Progress) Describe how to use a right-hand rule to find the field direction around a straight current-carrying wire.

answer.html: Imagine grasping the wire with your right hand with your thumb pointing in the direction of the conventional (positive) current. Your fingers curl around the wire in the direction of the magnetic field.

items.title: 16 (Check Your Progress) Iron filings on glass above an active electromagnet form a pattern. What difference is observed if the current is reversed?

body.html: Reversing the current reverses the direction of the field, but filings align along the field line either way, because each filing becomes a small magnet that lines up with the field in whichever sense it points.
The strength and the shape of the field are the same; only the arrowheads of the field lines would be reversed. The filings do not have arrowheads.

answer.html: No observable difference: the filings form the same pattern. (A compass would show the change, because its needle would point the opposite way.)

items.title: 17 (Check Your Progress) What happens to the domains of a temporary magnet when it is removed from a magnetic field?

answer.html: The domains return to a random arrangement, so their fields cancel out and the object loses its magnetization.

items.title: 18 (Check Your Progress, Critical Thinking) Toy with two parallel horizontal rods Problem 18(a) The top rod floats above the lower rod, but falls onto it when the top rod is reversed. Explain.

body.html: Rods that attract or repel by themselves are permanent magnets, and the force depends on which poles face each other.

Both rods are bar magnets. The top rod floats because the lower rod repels it: like poles face each other along their lengths, and magnetic repulsion supports the top rod's weight. Turning the top rod around swaps its poles, so unlike poles now face each other, and they attract. The top rod then falls onto the lower one.

answer.html: Both rods are permanent magnets with like poles facing in the floating arrangement (repulsion holds the rod up). Reversing the top rod puts unlike poles facing, which attracts, so it falls.

items.title: 18(b) A replacement top rod falls on the bottom rod no matter its orientation. What material is it?

body.html: A ferromagnetic material that is not magnetized is attracted by both poles of a magnet, because the magnet induces an opposite pole nearest to itself.
The rod is attracted either way it faces, so it has no poles of its own.

answer.html: An unmagnetized ferromagnetic material such as iron or steel (a temporary magnet by induction), not a permanent magnet.
